name: Cearense Portuguese
notes: Cearense (Fortaleza). Pretonic /e o/ open to [ɛ ɔ] before an open, nasal or low stressed vowel (Mota & Lopes 2018: 215). /t d/ affricate before [i]: ALiB rates Fortaleza categorical (Battisti & Dornelles Filho 2015: 226). Coda /S/ is alveolar (Marins & Margotti 2012: 257), aspirated before /d n/ in popular speech (Toledo & Cantoni 2021: 27). Coda /R/ is the aspirate [h] and is deleted word-finally (Callou, Serra & Cunha 2015: 197, 207).

allophone_rules.notes: Mota & Lopes (2018: 215, ALiB, North and Northeast capitals): pretonic mid vowels 'têm uma maior probabilidade de se tornarem médias abertas no contexto de tônica também de timbre aberto (médias-baixas), médias nasais e diante da vogal baixa [a]'; before a close-mid stressed vowel they stay closed in 86 % (/e/) and 91 % (/o/) of tokens. The trigger is the vowel two graphemes to the right, so a pretonic syllable closed by a consonant (espera) keeps the closed vowel.

Mota & Lopes (2018: 215, ALiB, North and Northeast capitals): pretonic mid vowels 'têm uma maior probabilidade de se tornarem médias abertas no contexto de tônica também de timbre aberto (médias-baixas), médias nasais e diante da vogal baixa [a]'; before a close-mid stressed vowel they stay closed in 86 % (/e/) and 91 % (/o/) of tokens. The trigger is the vowel two graphemes to the right, so a pretonic syllable closed by a consonant (espera) keeps the closed vowel.

Callou, Serra & Cunha (2015: 207, ALiB, Northeast capitals): word-final /R/ deletion reaches 94-98 % in verbs and 62-95 % in other words in every capital. Coda /R/ elsewhere is the aspirate [h]: the norm in these capitals is '[- vibrante] e [- anterior]' (p. 197).

Toledo & Cantoni (2021: 27) report Roncarati & Uchôa (2014), Fortaleza DSC corpus: 16.1 % aspiration overall, and 52 % before /d/ and 61 % before /n/, the two contexts where it is the majority. ALiB gives Fortaleza only 2 % aspiration (ibid.), and Fortaleza keeps the alveolar 'em qualquer contexto' (Marins & Margotti 2012: 257, quoting Jesus & Mota 2007); the rule models the popular speech of the DSC corpus. [d͡ʒ] is listed because a /d/ before [i] affricates first (desde).
